title: You almost lost your soul in the quietest way possible.
paragraphs: You almost lost your soul in the quietest way possible.
Not through scandal.
Not through rebellion.
Not through some public fall everyone could point at.
But through the slow, hidden poison of believing the blessing proved you were untouchable.

Hezekiah had prayed with his face to the wall. He had wept before God. He had received mercy when death was at his door. The Lord added fifteen years to his life, and for a moment, it looked like gratitude would become his legacy.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Sometimes the miracle you prayed for becomes the place where pride tests you.
When the envoys from Babylon came, Hezekiah showed them everything.
The silver.
The gold.
The spices.
The armory.
The treasures.
Nothing was hidden from them.
And Scripture says, “Hezekiah was glad of them, and showed them the house of his precious things” (Isaiah 39:2).
Read that again.
He was glad.
Not guarded.
Not prayerful.
Not trembling before the God who had spared him.
Glad.
There is a kind of pride that does not shout, “I don’t need God.”
It whispers, “Look how far I’ve come.”
God saw it.
You knew.

You knew when your testimony slowly became your trophy. You knew when the gift started getting more attention than the Giver. You knew when you stopped saying, “God had mercy on me,” and started making people admire what mercy produced.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
And the prophet Isaiah came with a question that still cuts today:
“What have they seen in your house?” (Isaiah 39:4)
Not just your home.
Your heart.
Your motives.
Your private altar.
What have people seen in you lately?
Have they seen Christ, or just your success dressed in spiritual language?
Hezekiah answered, “All that is in mine house have they seen.”
And judgment followed.
Because pride always opens doors humility would have kept shut.

But the Gospel does not leave us exposed without hope. Jesus Christ, the true and better King, had all glory, yet humbled Himself. Philippians 2 says He “made himself of no reputation” and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
Hezekiah showed his treasures.
Jesus gave Himself as the treasure.
Hezekiah’s pride pointed to coming ruin.
Jesus’ humility opened the way to redemption.

So repent before pride becomes normal. Turn while conviction still hurts. Come back to the cross where sinners are not polished but forgiven, not praised but cleansed, not admired but made new by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
